Breathe out fully — you should sink slowly.
Add or remove weight in small increments until that is what happens.
Remember a near-empty cylinder is 2-3 kg more buoyant, so add that much for the end of the dive.
Note the final figure with the suit, water type and cylinder in your log (221).
instructions.afterUse: Record it. Salt versus fresh, 5mm versus 7mm, steel versus aluminium all change the answer.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Descent Routine and Equalisation
instructions.description: Getting down in control, with ears that are happy.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Never force equalisation and never continue down against pain. Never dive with a cold or blocked sinuses — reverse block on ascent is the serious version of this problem.
steps: Signal to your buddy and agree to descend.
Start equalising at the surface, before you are under, and keep ahead of it.
Deflate the BCD with the inflator held high, and breathe out to start down.
Descend feet-first and slowly for the first few metres.
Equalise gently every metre — earlier and more often than feels necessary.
If an ear will not clear, stop, ascend a metre, and try again.
If it still will not clear, abort. There is no dive worth an ear.
Watch your buddy and stay together throughout.
Level off above the bottom and establish neutral buoyancy before doing anything else.
instructions.notes: Equalise before you feel pressure, not after. Once it hurts you are already behind.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Buoyancy and Trim Tuning
instructions.description: Working on the skill that makes every other skill easier.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Practise over sand or in mid-water, never over reef or anything fragile.
steps: Get properly weighted first (204). No amount of technique fixes 4 kg of extra lead.
Establish neutral at your working depth, then stop touching the inflator.
Control small changes with your lungs alone — inhale to rise, exhale to sink.
Hover motionless for a full minute without sculling. If you are finning to stay put, you are not neutral.
Check trim: aim for flat and horizontal, not head-up.
If your feet sink, move weight higher; if they float, move weight lower or use ankle weights.
Practise a fin pivot: neutral on an exhale, rising on an inhale, pivoting on your fin tips.
Practise stopping and holding depth at a signal from your buddy.
Add small amounts of gas on descent and vent early on ascent — always ahead of the change.
instructions.afterUse: Note weight and trim changes in the log so you do not solve the same problem twice (221).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Air Consumption Monitoring
instructions.description: Knowing how much gas you have and what it means.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Agree turn pressure and reserve before you get in, not underwater. Rule of thirds for anything overhead or with a long return.
steps: Check your gauge before entry and confirm the starting pressure with your buddy.
Check within the first few minutes at depth, then roughly every five minutes.
Check every single time your depth changes significantly.
Signal your pressure to your buddy at agreed intervals, not just when asked.
Turn the dive at the agreed turn pressure, regardless of how good it is down there.
Begin the ascent with the agreed reserve still in the cylinder.
Surface with a genuine reserve — commonly 50 bar, more in cold water or current.
Note start and end pressures and dive time in your log to build your real SAC rate.
instructions.afterUse: Calculate your consumption rate over time. Knowing your own number turns dive planning from guesswork into arithmetic.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Safety Stop Routine
instructions.description: The three minutes that matter at the end of the dive.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. A safety stop is standard practice on any dive to any meaningful depth, not an optional extra when convenient.
steps: Begin the ascent with enough gas to complete the stop comfortably (207).
Ascend slowly and level off at 5 metres — or as your computer directs.
Establish neutral buoyancy and hold the depth without a line if you can.
Hold for a full three minutes, longer if the dive was deep or repetitive.
Stay with your buddy and stay at the same depth as each other.
Watch your computer for depth drift — the surge at 5 metres will move you.
Deploy an SMB before or during the stop if there is any boat traffic.
Complete the last 5 metres slower than the rest of the ascent, taking a full minute.
instructions.notes: The shallowest part of the ascent is where the greatest pressure change happens. Slowest at the end.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Ascent Routine
instructions.description: Coming up in a controlled, predictable way.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Never hold your breath on ascent, at any depth, for any reason. Never exceed your computer's ascent rate.
steps: Signal the ascent to your buddy and get acknowledgement.
Check your gas and your computer before starting up.
Look up and reach up. Keep turning to check the surface above you.
Ascend at no more than the rate your computer allows — commonly 9-10 m/min, slower is better.
Vent gas from the BCD continuously as you rise, staying ahead of the expansion.
Stay within arm's reach of your buddy.
Complete the safety stop (208).
Deploy the SMB if you are not on a line and there is any traffic.
Break the surface looking up, then inflate the BCD and signal OK to the boat or shore.
instructions.afterUse: Stay together on the surface until you are both out.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Dive Planning
instructions.description: Agreeing the dive before it happens.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Plan the dive and dive the plan. Anyone can call the dive at any time, for any reason, with no argument and no questions.
steps: Agree the objective: what are you actually going to do down there.
Agree maximum depth and maximum time, and make them limits not targets.
Check the computer's no-stop time for that depth, and your residual nitrogen from earlier dives.
Agree turn pressure and minimum surfacing reserve (207).
Agree the route and the navigation plan (220).
Agree entry and exit points, and the alternates if conditions change.
Agree lost-buddy procedure: search for one minute, then surface.
Review the emergency plan: nearest oxygen, nearest phone, emergency numbers, nearest chamber.
Check conditions on the day: current, visibility, surface state, tide, forecast.
Confirm everyone is fit to dive — sleep, alcohol, illness, medication.
instructions.afterUse: If the conditions do not match the plan, replan or do not dive.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Boat Dive Entry and Exit
instructions.description: Getting off and back onto a boat without incident.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Never enter the water until the crew says so. Propellers and moving boats are the hazard here, not the diving.
steps: Listen to the full boat briefing and ask if anything is unclear.
Kit up in your allocated spot and stay seated with the cylinder supported.
Buddy check while seated (201).
Stand only when told, and move to the entry point holding on.
At the entry point: mask on and defogged, reg in, one hand on mask and reg, other on weight belt.
Look to the crew for the signal and check the water below is clear.
Giant stride or backward roll as briefed, and keep everything held down.
On the surface, signal OK immediately and move clear of the entry point.
On exit: approach the ladder one at a time, never underneath another diver.
Remove fins at the ladder and pass them up, or as the crew directs.
Hold the ladder with both hands and climb steadily. Sit down before removing anything.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Shore Dive Entry and Exit
instructions.description: Getting in and out through surf, rocks or a slipway.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. The entry and exit are the most dangerous parts of most shore dives. Watch the site for ten minutes before committing.
steps: Watch the water first: wave sets, timing, surge, and where the rocks actually are.
Identify your exit point before you enter, and a backup exit further along.
Note a shore landmark you can recognise from the water.
Kit up above the waterline, but do not walk far in full kit — carry fins and put them on at the water.
Enter with mask on, reg in, and BCD partly inflated.
Walk in backwards or sideways in surf, never forwards.
Once deep enough, put fins on in the water while holding your buddy.
Swim out beyond the break before descending.
On exit, wait outside the break, watch for a lull, then come in on the back of a wave.
Keep the reg in until you are standing on dry land.
Crawl rather than stand if the surge is knocking you over.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Mask Clearing Drill
instructions.where: Shallow water or start of a dive
instructions.description: Keeping the skill fresh so a flooded mask is a non-event.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Practise shallow, neutrally buoyant, with your buddy watching. Keep breathing normally throughout — never hold your breath.
steps: Establish neutral buoyancy and signal your buddy what you are practising.
Keep breathing steadily from the regulator the whole time.
Partially flood: pull the top seal away, let a little water in, then clear it.
To clear: press the top of the mask against your forehead, look slightly up, and exhale steadily through the nose.
Repeat with a full flood.
Then remove the mask entirely, hold it, breathe normally for several breaths with eyes closed or open.
Refit the mask, clear the strap of hair, and clear it fully.
Repeat until it feels boring, which is the point.
instructions.notes: The instinct to hold your breath is the thing being trained out. Slow, continuous breathing is the whole skill.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Regulator Recovery Drill
instructions.description: Getting the regulator back when it is knocked from your mouth.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Exhale a small continuous stream of bubbles whenever the regulator is out of your mouth. Never hold your breath.
steps: Neutral buoyancy, buddy watching, signal what you are practising.
Remove the regulator and immediately begin a slow continuous exhale.
Arm sweep method: lean right, drop the right shoulder, sweep the right arm from the thigh backwards and out in a wide arc.
The hose should catch on your arm. Follow it to the second stage.
Replace it and clear it — either purge briefly, or exhale sharply into it.
Take a cautious first breath, then resume normal breathing.
Now the reach method: reach behind the right shoulder to the first stage and follow the hose down.
Practise both. In real life you will use whichever your body finds first.
Finish by practising with the alternate as well.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Out-of-Air Response Drill
instructions.description: Rehearsing the sequence so it happens without thinking.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. This is a drill, practised shallow and calm. The real prevention is gas monitoring (207) — a drill is the last line, not the plan.
steps: Agree with your buddy exactly what you are rehearsing and the signals.
Practise the out-of-air signal — a flat hand drawn across the throat — until it is instant.
Donor: present the alternate immediately, second stage first, facing the recipient correctly.
Recipient: take it, clear it, breathe. Exhale continuously during the swap.
Both: establish a firm grip on each other, forearm to forearm.
Agree the ascent and go up together at a controlled rate, venting as you rise (209).
Include a safety stop if gas allows.
Also rehearse the controlled emergency swimming ascent: continuous exhale, ahhhh sound, looking up, from shallow depth only.
Swap roles and repeat.
instructions.afterUse: Discuss what went wrong afterwards. Something always does, and that is the value of a drill.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cramp and Leg Fatigue Management
instructions.description: Dealing with cramp underwater without turning it into a problem.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Signal your buddy before you deal with it. Do not sort it out silently while they swim off.
steps: Signal your buddy and stop.
Establish neutral buoyancy so you are not sinking or rising while distracted.
Grab the tip of the fin on the cramping leg and pull it steadily towards you, straightening the leg.
Hold the stretch for 20-30 seconds.
Massage the muscle if you can reach it.
Rest, then swim gently. Change your kick style — switch to a frog kick to use different muscles.
If it recurs, call the dive and ascend normally with your buddy.
On the surface, get support from the buddy or a line, and stretch again.
instructions.afterUse: Cramp is usually hydration, electrolytes, cold or over-finning. Drink properly before diving and do not fin hard against current.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Night Dive Preparation
instructions.description: The extra preparation a dive after dark needs.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Do not night dive a site you have not dived in daylight. Two lights minimum per diver, always.
steps: Dive the site in daylight first, the same day if possible.
Primary torch plus a backup torch, both tested with fresh batteries or full charge.
Fit a marker light to each cylinder valve, and agree who has which colour.
Agree light signals before entry: OK, attention, problem, and how to signal without dazzling.
Never shine a light into anyone's face — signal by circling the beam on the seabed.
Agree a much tighter buddy distance than in daylight.
Mark the entry and exit point with a light from the shore or boat.
Plan a shallower, shorter, simpler dive than you would in daylight.
Brief the surface party on timings and when to be concerned.
Check the surface conditions and the moon and tide state.
instructions.afterUse: Surface with more reserve than usual. Everything takes longer in the dark.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Drift Dive Procedure
instructions.description: Diving with the current rather than against it.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Never try to swim against a current. If you are separated from the group, deploy your SMB and surface — the boat follows the bubbles and the buoy.
steps: Listen to the skipper's briefing on the current direction, strength and the pick-up plan.
Confirm everyone has an SMB and reel, and can deploy it.
Negative or rapid entry as briefed, so the group stays together at the start.
Descend immediately and together — the group splits at the surface, not the bottom.
Go with the current. Use reef hooks or shelter behind structure to pause, if permitted.
Stay in a tight group; visibility of your buddy matters more than usual.
Monitor gas more frequently — current work uses more than you expect (207).
Deploy the SMB before ascending, from depth, and ascend up the line.
Complete the safety stop while drifting, watching the computer for depth (208).
On the surface, stay together, signal, and wait for the boat to come to you.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cold Water and Drysuit Routine
instructions.description: Diving cold without misery or incident.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Drysuit diving needs specific training — the suit is a second buoyancy device and can invert you. Do not use one without the course.
steps: Check the suit seals and zip before the dive; wax or lubricate the zip as the maker says.
Dress in the right undersuit for the water temperature, not the air temperature.
Test the inflate and dump valves before entry, and set the shoulder dump to auto.
Purge air from the suit before descending by squatting and opening the shoulder dump.
On descent, add small amounts of gas to the suit to offset the squeeze.
Use the BCD for buoyancy and the suit only for comfort — pick one and be consistent.
Keep your feet down; air migrating to the boots is what causes an inverted ascent.
On ascent, vent the suit early and continuously.
Watch for cold: shivering, clumsiness or poor judgement ends the dive immediately.
Rewarm gradually afterwards, with warm drinks and dry layers.
instructions.afterUse: Hang the suit inside out to dry the undersuit and the seals, out of sunlight (223).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Underwater Navigation
instructions.description: Knowing where you are and getting back.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Agree the navigation plan before entry. Getting lost is a gas problem before it is anything else.
instructions.equipment: Compass, slate, timing device
steps: Set your heading on the surface before descending and note the reciprocal.
Hold the compass level and square to your body; turn your whole body, not your wrist.
Count fin kicks or use elapsed time to measure distance — pick one and stay consistent.
Note natural features as you go: sand ripples run parallel to shore, depth contours, prominent structures.
Note the direction of any current and how it will affect the return.
For an out-and-back, turn on the reciprocal heading at your turn point.
For a square, make three 90-degree turns with equal legs.
Cross-check depth against your plan — depth is the most reliable navigation aid there is.
Surface early rather than searching. It is not a failure.
instructions.afterUse: Sketch the site in your log afterwards. Second dives at the same site are far better for it (221).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Dive Log Completion
instructions.description: Recording the dive while it is still fresh.
steps: Fill it in on the boat or the shore, not three weeks later.
Record: date, site, entry and exit time, max depth, average depth, bottom time.
Record start and end pressure, and calculate gas used.
Record water temperature at depth and at the surface.
Record the exposure suit and the exact weight carried — this is the entry you will look up most (204).
Record visibility, current and surface conditions.
Record buddy and any certifications or signatures needed.
Note what you saw, and sketch the site if you navigated it (220).
Note anything about the kit: what worked, what needs fixing.
Note anything about yourself: how the gas consumption felt, any equalisation issues.
instructions.afterUse: Review the log before diving the same site or the same conditions again.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Post-Dive Flying and Altitude
instructions.description: The surface interval before flying or driving over mountains.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. This is a genuine decompression risk, not a formality. Follow your computer and your agency guidance, and when they differ, take the longer interval.
steps: Plan the last dive of the trip around the flight, not the other way round.
Common guidance: at least 12 hours after a single no-stop dive, 18 hours after multiple days of diving or any dive requiring stops.
If your computer gives a no-fly countdown, use it and do not second-guess it downwards.
The same applies to driving over a mountain pass — altitude is altitude.
Do not dive at all on the day of a flight.
Stay hydrated and avoid alcohol during the surface interval.
Avoid hard exercise and hot tubs in the hours after diving.
Know where the nearest chamber is, and carry your dive insurance details.
instructions.notes: RV travel makes this relevant twice over: a dive trip followed by an alpine drive needs the same interval as a flight.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Wetsuit and Drysuit Care
instructions.description: Making an expensive suit last.
instructions.warnings: Sunlight destroys neoprene and latex faster than anything else. Dry in the shade, always.
steps: Rinse in fresh water as soon as possible after the dive, inside and out.
For a wetsuit, turn it inside out and rinse the inside properly — that is where the salt and sweat is.
Use a proper wetsuit shampoo occasionally, never household detergent.
Hang on a wide hanger, never a thin wire one which creases the shoulders.
Dry inside out first, then turn and dry the outside.
Never in direct sun, never on a radiator, never in a tumble dryer.
Drysuit: rinse the zip and lubricate it with the recommended wax while it is clean.
Drysuit: treat latex seals with talc or the recommended product; check for small tears at the wrists.
Store hanging or loosely rolled, never folded on a crease, and never compressed.
Check the suit before the next trip rather than at the dive site.
instructions.maintenance: Repair small nicks in neoprene with wetsuit glue immediately — they always grow.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Dive Computer Setup and Battery
instructions.description: Making sure the computer is set for the dive you are actually doing.
instructions.warnings: These are personal reminders, not training. Dive only within the limits of your certification, your currency and the conditions on the day. If anything here differs from your agency training or the local briefing, follow the training and the briefing. Never share a computer between divers, and never dive on a computer that has been switched off between repetitive dives — it loses your tissue loading.
steps: Check the battery level before every dive day, and carry a spare battery or charger.
Set the correct gas mix. If you are on nitrox, analyse the cylinder yourself and set the actual figure.
Set the maximum PO2 limit you intend to use.
Set the correct water type — salt or fresh — as it affects depth accuracy.
Set the altitude mode if you are diving above sea level, including alpine lakes.
Set conservatism to suit the day: cold, hard work, tiredness, age and repetitive diving all argue for more.
Check the ascent rate alarm is enabled.
Check date and time are correct so the log and surface intervals are right.
Confirm no residual no-fly or desaturation time is showing from previous dives.
Wear it on the same wrist every time so reading it is automatic.
instructions.maintenance: Change the battery before a trip, not during. Pressure-test after a battery change if the maker recommends it.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Dynamic Warm-Up for Running
instructions.description: Ten minutes that make the first kilometre feel like the fifth.
instructions.warnings: No static stretching before running. Hold-and-stretch belongs afterwards; before, you want movement.
instructions.preparations: Do this indoors or at the start of the run, not after standing around in the cold.
steps: Walk briskly for 3 minutes to raise the temperature.
Leg swings forward and back, 10 each leg, holding something for balance.
Leg swings side to side, 10 each leg.
Walking lunges, 10 each side, with a gentle twist towards the front leg.
Hip circles, 10 each direction.
Ankle circles and 15 calf raises.
High knees, 20 steps.
Butt kicks, 20 steps.
A-skips, 20 metres.
Start running easy for the first 5 minutes regardless of the session — the session starts after that.
instructions.afterUse: Go straight into the run while warm. Standing around undoes it in three minutes.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Easy Run — Aerobic Base
instructions.description: The steady conversational run that builds most of your fitness.
instructions.warnings: The classic mistake is running easy days too hard. If you cannot hold a conversation, you are not running easy.
steps: Warm up (300).
Settle into a pace where you could speak in full sentences.
Breathe through the nose if you can — it is a useful check on effort.
Keep it there even when you feel good. Especially when you feel good.
On hills, keep the effort even rather than the pace — slow down going up.
Aim for 45-75 minutes depending on where you are in the week.
Finish feeling like you could do it again.
Cool down and stretch (302).
instructions.notes: Roughly 80% of weekly running should be at this effort. It is the least glamorous and most important session.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cool-Down and Post-Run Routine
instructions.description: The ten minutes after the run that decide how tomorrow feels.
steps: Do not stop dead. Jog very easily for 5 minutes, then walk for 3.
Let the heart rate come down before you sit.
Now static stretches, held 30 seconds each, no bouncing.
Calves — both straight-leg and bent-knee versions.
Hamstrings, one leg at a time.
Quads, holding something for balance.
Hip flexors in a half-kneeling lunge — the one runners need most and skip most.
Glutes, figure-four seated or lying.
IT band and outer hip.
Rehydrate, and eat something with protein and carbohydrate within the hour.
Get out of wet kit promptly.
instructions.afterUse: Note the run: distance, time, effort, and how you felt. The last one is the useful one.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Interval Session — 400m Repeats
instructions.description: Short, fast repeats for speed and running economy.
instructions.warnings: This is a hard session. Not on consecutive days with another hard session, and not when you are already tired or unwell.
instructions.preparations: Full warm-up first — this session punishes a cold start.
steps: Warm up thoroughly: 15 minutes easy jog plus the dynamic routine (300).
Add 4 strides of 80m building to fast, with full recovery (310).
Run 400m at roughly your current 5k race effort — hard but controlled, not a sprint.
Recover 90 seconds jogging, not standing.
Repeat 8-12 times depending on your level. Start with 6 if new to it.
The target is even splits — the last one should match the first.
If the pace drops by more than a few seconds, stop the session. Quality over quantity.
Cool down 10-15 minutes easy jog, then stretch (302).
instructions.afterUse: Log every split. Progress here is very visible over a few weeks.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Interval Session — 1km Repeats
instructions.where: Track, path or measured road loop
instructions.description: Longer intervals for sustained speed and mental toughness.
instructions.warnings: Hard session. Allow 48 hours before another hard one.
steps: Warm up 15 minutes easy plus dynamic drills (300).
Add 4 strides with full recovery.
Run 1km at around 10k race effort — comfortably hard, sustainable, not flat out.
Recover 2-3 minutes with easy jogging.
Repeat 4-6 times.
Hold the pace steady; the discipline is not going out too fast on the first one.
Focus on relaxed shoulders and a quick cadence as fatigue arrives.
Cool down 10-15 minutes easy, then stretch (302).
instructions.notes: If you can only just finish the last rep at pace, you got it right. If you had two more in you, go slightly faster next time.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Tempo / Threshold Run
instructions.description: The comfortably-hard sustained effort that raises your threshold.
instructions.warnings: Tempo is not a race. If you are gasping, you have gone past threshold and you are doing a different, less useful session.
steps: Warm up 15 minutes easy plus drills (300).
Settle into an effort you could hold for about an hour in a race — roughly half-marathon pace.
The talk test: you can say a short sentence, not a paragraph.
Hold it for 20-30 minutes continuously.
Alternatively break it into 2 x 15 minutes with 3 minutes easy between, which is easier to hold cleanly.
Keep the effort even, especially over undulations.
Focus on rhythm and relaxed breathing rather than the watch.
Cool down 10-15 minutes easy, then stretch (302).
instructions.notes: This is the single most productive session for anyone racing 10k to marathon.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Long Slow Run
instructions.where: Route with water access or carried
instructions.description: The weekly long one that builds endurance.
instructions.warnings: Increase long-run distance by no more than about 10% a week, and take a shorter one every fourth week.
instructions.equipment: Water, gel or snack if over 90 minutes, phone, weather-appropriate layers
instructions.preparations: Eat properly 2-3 hours before. Plan the route and tell someone where you are going.
steps: Start slower than feels right. Genuinely slower.
Hold an easy conversational effort throughout (301).
Drink to thirst from the start rather than catching up later.
Take on carbohydrate every 40-45 minutes if the run is over 90 minutes.
Walk the steep hills if it keeps the effort where it should be.
Practise your race-day fuelling and kit on these runs — nothing new on race day.
Finish the last 10 minutes slightly quicker only if you feel strong.
Cool down, stretch, and eat within 30 minutes (302).
instructions.afterUse: The long run is where fatigue accumulates. Take the following day easy or off.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Hill Repeats
instructions.where: A hill of 200-400m at a steady gradient
instructions.description: Strength and power without going to a gym.
instructions.warnings: The downhill is where injuries happen, not the uphill. Jog down loose and easy, never race it.
steps: Find a hill of 200-400m with a consistent 5-8% gradient.
Warm up 15 minutes easy on the flat plus drills (300).
Run up at a hard but controlled effort — think 5k effort, not a sprint.
Drive the arms, shorten the stride, lift the knees, look up the hill not at your feet.
Jog back down slowly and completely relaxed. That is the recovery.
Repeat 6-10 times.
Stop when the form breaks down rather than when the count is reached.
Cool down 10 minutes flat and easy, then stretch (302).
instructions.notes: Hill repeats are resistance training disguised as running. Excellent for anyone short on time.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Fartlek Session
instructions.description: Unstructured speed play — the fun hard session.
steps: Warm up 10-15 minutes easy plus drills (300).
Pick a landmark ahead — a tree, a lamppost, a bend — and run hard to it.
Recover easy until you feel ready, not for a fixed time.
Pick another landmark and go again.
Vary the length deliberately: some 20 seconds, some 3 minutes.
Use the terrain — surge on the hills, float on the descents.
Keep it playful. This session is meant to be enjoyable and not measured.
20-30 minutes of this, then cool down and stretch (302).
instructions.notes: Good for weeks when structure feels like a burden, and excellent on holiday or in unfamiliar places.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Progression Run
instructions.description: Starting easy and finishing strong.
steps: Warm up 10 minutes easy (300).
Divide the run into three equal thirds.
First third: easy conversational pace (301).
Second third: steady — noticeably working, still comfortable.
Final third: tempo effort, comfortably hard (305).
Each transition should feel deliberate, not accidental.
Finish the last few minutes at the strongest sustainable effort.
Cool down 10 minutes easy, then stretch (302).
instructions.notes: Excellent pacing practice. Most people race the first half too hard, and this teaches the opposite habit.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Strides and Accelerations
instructions.description: Short, fast, relaxed efforts that improve form without fatigue.
instructions.warnings: Strides are not sprints. If you are straining, you are doing them too hard.
steps: Do these after an easy run, or as part of a warm-up before a hard session.
Accelerate smoothly over about 20 metres.
Hold near-top-end relaxed speed for about 40 metres.
Decelerate gradually over the last 20 metres.
Focus on quick feet, tall posture, relaxed jaw and hands.
Walk or jog back for full recovery — 60-90 seconds.
Repeat 4-6 times.
Stop if the form degrades at all.
instructions.notes: A few strides twice a week keeps the legs sharp during high-mileage phases and costs almost nothing in fatigue.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Recovery Run
instructions.description: A run so easy it feels pointless, which is the point.
instructions.warnings: If you cannot resist running this faster, take the day off instead. A recovery run run hard is worse than nothing.
steps: Keep it short — 20-40 minutes maximum.
Run slower than your easy pace. Slower still.
Nose breathing throughout, comfortably.
Soft surface if you can: grass, trail, track.
Leave the watch at home or cover the screen.
Focus on relaxed, smooth form.
Stop if anything hurts. This run has no training value worth an injury.
Stretch afterwards (302).
instructions.notes: The purpose is blood flow and habit, not fitness. Ego is the only obstacle.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Treadmill Session
instructions.description: Making indoor running useful rather than tedious.
instructions.warnings: Straddle the belt to start and stop. Always clip the safety key to yourself.
steps: Set 1% incline as the baseline to approximate outdoor effort.
Warm up 10 minutes with the pace building gradually.
Structure the session so you are not just staring at the numbers — intervals work well indoors.
Example: 8 x 3 minutes at threshold with 90 seconds easy between.
Or a progression: increase 0.5 km/h every 5 minutes.
Or a hill session: hold pace and increase the gradient 1% every 2 minutes.
Have a fan on you and drink more than you think — you sweat more indoors.
Cool down 5-10 minutes with the pace dropping, then stretch (302).
instructions.notes: Useful for the RV or a hotel, in bad weather, or for holding a precise pace.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Trail Run Preparation
instructions.description: Getting ready for running off-road, safely.
instructions.warnings: Tell someone your route and expected return time. Phone signal on trails is not something to rely on.
instructions.equipment: Trail shoes, water, phone, whistle, layer, map or GPS, small first aid kit
steps: Check the weather including on the tops, not just at the trailhead.
Plan the route and note the escape options.
Tell someone the route and your expected time back.
Wear trail shoes with real grip — road shoes on wet rock is how ankles go.
Carry water, a layer, a phone and something to eat.
Start conservatively; trail effort is much higher than road for the same pace.
Walk the steep climbs without guilt — everyone does.
Shorten the stride on descents, look 3-4 metres ahead rather than at your feet.
Turn back at the time you agreed rather than the point you hoped to reach.
instructions.afterUse: Wash the shoes and dry them away from direct heat.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Running Form Check
instructions.where: Track, treadmill or with a phone camera
instructions.description: A periodic look at how you are actually running.
steps: Film yourself from the side and from behind, at easy pace, for 20 seconds.
Cadence: count right foot strikes for 30 seconds and double it, then double again. Aim roughly 170-180 total.
Posture: a slight lean from the ankles, not from the waist. Head level, eyes ahead.
Foot strike: landing under the body, not out in front. This matters more than heel versus forefoot.
Arms: driving back not across the body, elbows around 90 degrees, hands relaxed.
Shoulders: down and loose. Check them mid-run and drop them.
Hips: level, not dropping on one side — that is a glute strength issue (906).
Pick ONE thing to change and work on it for a few weeks. Not five.
instructions.afterUse: Refilm in a month and compare rather than relying on how it felt.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Race Morning Routine
instructions.description: The morning of, planned so nothing is improvised.
instructions.warnings: Nothing new on race day. Not shoes, not food, not gels, not socks. Nothing.
instructions.preparations: Lay everything out the night before, including pinned-on number and timing chip.
steps: Wake at least 3 hours before the start.
Eat your normal pre-race breakfast — the one you have practised on long runs.
Drink steadily but do not overdo it.
Arrive early enough to be unhurried: toilet queues are always longer than you plan for.
Warm up appropriately: longer and fuller for a 5k, barely anything for a marathon.
Dynamic drills and a few strides for shorter races (300, 310).
Keep warm until as late as possible; take a throwaway layer.
Get into the right start pen and do not start too far forward.
First kilometre deliberately slower than target pace.
Run your own race, not the pace of whoever is beside you.
instructions.afterUse: Keep moving after finishing, get warm and dry, eat within 30 minutes.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Taper Week
instructions.description: Backing off before a race so the training arrives on the day.
instructions.warnings: The taper is where fitness surfaces. Extra training now cannot help you and can absolutely hurt you.
steps: Reduce volume substantially — roughly 40-50% in the final week for a marathon, less for shorter races.
Keep the intensity: fewer hard reps, but at the same pace.
Keep the frequency: do not suddenly stop running.
Final hard session no later than 4-5 days out, and keep it short.
Expect to feel sluggish and slightly anxious mid-taper. That is normal and passes.
Sleep more; that is the real work of taper week.
Eat normally, increasing carbohydrate in the last two or three days.
Avoid new activities, long walks round a city, or anything that puts unusual load on the legs.
Lay out kit and plan logistics rather than training (315).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Hot Weather Running
instructions.description: Running in heat without ruining the session or yourself.
instructions.warnings: Heat exhaustion signs — stopping sweating, confusion, chills, nausea — mean stop immediately, get in the shade, get cool and get help. Do not push through.
steps: Run early morning or late evening, avoiding the middle of the day entirely.
Slow down. Expect to lose noticeable pace per kilometre for the same effort, and accept it.
Run by effort or heart rate, not pace.
Hydrate before, during and after; add electrolytes for anything over an hour.
Wear light-coloured, loose, technical fabric, plus a cap and sunglasses.
Sunscreen, reapplied for long runs.
Plan a route with shade and water, or loop past your car or home.
Pour water over your head and neck as well as drinking it.
Allow 10-14 days to acclimatise — the first hot week is the worst.
instructions.afterUse: Rehydrate with electrolytes, not just water, and check your weight change if the run was long.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cold Weather Running
instructions.description: Dressing and running for winter conditions.
instructions.warnings: On ice, do not run. Traction devices or a treadmill — a broken wrist costs a season.
steps: Dress for about 10°C warmer than it is. You should feel slightly cold for the first five minutes.
Layer: technical base, insulating mid, windproof outer. No cotton anywhere.
Cover the extremities — hat and gloves matter far more than another body layer.
Extend the warm-up and do it indoors (300).
Start into the wind so you finish with it behind you.
Shorten the stride on any slippery surface and keep the feet under you.
Be visible: reflective kit and a light in the dark.
Drink even though you do not feel thirsty — you dehydrate in the cold too.
Get out of wet kit immediately afterwards; the chill arrives fast once you stop.
instructions.afterUse: Warm shower and dry layers straight away. Do not stand around chatting in wet kit.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Running Shoe Rotation and Retirement
instructions.description: Tracking shoes so you replace them before they cause an injury.
instructions.warnings: Worn-out midsoles are a common cause of niggles that appear from nowhere. The upper looking fine means nothing.
steps: Write the purchase date inside each pair with a marker.
Log the mileage on each pair, or at least a rough count.
Retire most road shoes somewhere between 600 and 900 km.
Check the midsole for compression lines and creasing — that is the real wear indicator.
Check the outsole for wear through to the midsole, especially at the heel and forefoot.
Press the midsole with your thumb: if it feels dead and does not spring back, it is done.
Rotate between at least two pairs — it extends the life of both and varies the loading.
Match the shoe to the session: cushioned for long and easy, lighter for fast, trail for off-road.
Never race in shoes you have not run in.
instructions.afterUse: Old shoes become gardening or dog-walking shoes, not running shoes.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Pre-Ride Safety Check (M-Check)
instructions.description: The two-minute check that follows the shape of an M across the bike.
instructions.warnings: Do this every ride, not just before long ones. A loose quick-release is not something you notice at speed.
steps: Start at the front hub: check the quick-release or thru-axle is closed and tight, and the wheel spins true.
Up to the handlebars: check the bars and stem are tight, and the levers do not rotate.
Brakes: pull both levers hard — firm, not spongy, and the wheel must not turn.
Down to the bottom bracket: check the cranks have no play, and the pedals spin freely and are tight.
Up to the saddle: check it is tight, level and at the right height.
Down to the rear hub: same check as the front.
Chain: check it is clean, lubricated and running smoothly.
Tyres: pressure by thumb or gauge, and look for cuts, embedded glass and sidewall damage (414).
Lift the bike a few centimetres and drop it — listen for anything rattling.
Check you have: pump, tube, levers, multitool, phone, water.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Dynamic Warm-Up for Cycling
instructions.description: Getting the hips and legs ready before the pedals turn hard.
steps: Off the bike: leg swings forward and back, 10 each leg.
Hip circles, 10 each direction.
10 bodyweight squats, slow and full range.
10 walking lunges.
Arm and shoulder circles, 10 each way — the upper body takes load on the bike too.
On the bike: 10 minutes spinning easy in a low gear at 90+ rpm.
3 x 30 seconds gradually building effort, with 90 seconds easy between.
2 x 15 second high-cadence spin-ups above 110 rpm.
Then start the session proper.
instructions.notes: A longer warm-up before hard sessions, and a much longer one when it is cold.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Endurance Ride — Zone 2
instructions.description: The long steady ride that builds the aerobic engine.
instructions.warnings: The temptation is to ride the flat bits too hard and the hills too hard. Keep the effort even and boring.
instructions.equipment: Two bottles, food for anything over 90 minutes, spares, phone, layers
steps: Warm up 15 minutes easy (401).
Settle into an effort you could sustain for hours — able to talk in sentences.
Keep cadence around 85-95 rpm; do not grind big gears.
On climbs, drop gears and keep the effort steady rather than the speed.
Eat 60-90g of carbohydrate an hour on anything over 90 minutes, starting early.
Drink 500-750ml an hour, more in heat.
Stay in the zone even when you feel strong — that is the discipline of the session.
Cool down the last 10 minutes spinning easy (403).
instructions.notes: This is the majority of your riding volume. It should feel almost too easy.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cool-Down After a Ride
instructions.description: Finishing properly rather than just stopping.
steps: Spin easy in a low gear at high cadence for the last 10 minutes of the ride.
Off the bike, walk for 2-3 minutes before sitting down.
Stretch: hip flexors in a half-kneeling lunge — the biggest one for cyclists.
Quads, standing, holding something.
Hamstrings.
Glutes, figure-four.
Calves, both straight and bent knee.
Chest and shoulders in a doorway — the counter to hours in the drops.
Neck side to side, gently.
Rehydrate and eat within 30 minutes.
Get out of the wet kit; do not sit around in a damp chamois.
instructions.afterUse: Wipe the bike down while the kit is in the wash (418).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Interval Session — 30/30s
instructions.description: Short, sharp repeats for top-end fitness.
instructions.warnings: Very hard session. Best done indoors or on a closed loop where you are not braking or navigating.
steps: Warm up thoroughly, 20 minutes including build efforts (401).
30 seconds hard — around 110-120% of threshold, a strong effort but repeatable.
30 seconds easy spinning.
Repeat 10 times to complete one block.
Recover 5 minutes very easy between blocks.
Complete 2-3 blocks.
Keep cadence high throughout, 95-105 rpm on the efforts.
The last rep of the last block should be the hardest thing you do, but completeable.
Cool down 10-15 minutes easy (403).
instructions.afterUse: Log the average power or speed per block. Consistency across blocks is the marker.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Threshold Session — 4 x 8 Minutes
instructions.description: The bread-and-butter session for raising sustainable power.
steps: Warm up 20 minutes with 2-3 short build efforts (401).
8 minutes at threshold — roughly the hardest effort you could hold for an hour.
It should feel comfortably hard for the first 3 minutes and genuinely hard by the last 2.
Recover 4 minutes easy spinning.
Repeat 4 times.
Hold the same effort on every interval; do not start the first one too hard.
Stay seated for most of it, standing only briefly to relieve pressure.
Cadence 85-95 rpm.
Cool down 10-15 minutes (403).
instructions.notes: If you can complete all four at the same effort with a little left, that is the session done correctly.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Sweet Spot Session
instructions.description: Just below threshold — high training benefit for manageable fatigue.
steps: Warm up 15-20 minutes (401).
Ride at around 88-94% of threshold effort — hard, but you could hold a short sentence.
Do 3 x 15 minutes, or 2 x 20 minutes for a bigger session.
Recover 5 minutes easy between efforts.
Keep the effort even; this session rewards discipline over heroics.
Cadence 85-95 rpm, staying seated.
Ideal on a steady climb or indoors where the effort is uninterrupted.
Cool down 10 minutes easy (403).
instructions.notes: The best value session when time is short — most of the threshold benefit, much less recovery cost.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: VO2 Max Session — 5 x 5 Minutes
instructions.description: The session that raises your ceiling.
instructions.warnings: The hardest session in the plan. Only when fresh, and never twice in a week alongside other hard work.
steps: Warm up 20-25 minutes with build efforts — a short warm-up ruins this session (401).
5 minutes at around 105-115% of threshold. Breathing should be heavy from about 90 seconds.
Recover 5 minutes very easy — equal recovery is essential here.
Repeat 5 times.
Pace the first interval properly: if you cannot complete the fifth, the first was too hard.
Cadence 90-100 rpm.
If you cannot hold the target on the fourth, stop at four. A failed fifth adds nothing.
Cool down 15 minutes easy (403).
instructions.afterUse: Expect to need an easy day after. Plan it in rather than discovering it.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Sprint Session
instructions.where: Safe flat road, no traffic, good surface
instructions.description: Maximum efforts for neuromuscular power.
instructions.warnings: Full-gas sprints demand a clear, straight, well-surfaced road with no junctions. Check the road each time before you go.
steps: Warm up 20 minutes with several building efforts (401).
From a moderate rolling speed, select a gear you can accelerate but not spin out.
Sprint all-out for 10-15 seconds, out of the saddle for the first few pedal strokes.
Keep the upper body still; pull on the bars against the pedal stroke.
Recover fully — 5 minutes minimum. This is a power session, not a fitness one.
Repeat 6-8 times.
Stop when peak power drops noticeably; the session is over at that point.
Practise both seated and standing starts.
Cool down 10-15 minutes (403).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Hill Climbing Session
instructions.description: Climbing repeats for strength and pacing.
instructions.warnings: On the descents: brake before the corner not in it, look where you want to go, and never overcook an unfamiliar bend.
steps: Warm up 20 minutes on the flat before the first climb (401).
Climb at threshold effort, seated for most of it (405).
Stand for 20-30 seconds every few minutes to change the muscle loading and relieve pressure.
Keep cadence at 70-85 rpm seated; do not let it fall below 60.
Stay near the front of the saddle and keep the upper body relaxed.
Descend carefully and completely — the descent is the recovery, not part of the session.
Repeat 3-5 times depending on the climb length.
Pace the first climb as if you had two more than you do.
Cool down on the flat, 10-15 minutes (403).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Long Ride Fuelling
instructions.description: Eating and drinking so the last hour is as good as the first.
instructions.warnings: The classic error is starting to eat when you feel hungry. By then it is too late — you are already behind.
instructions.equipment: Two bottles, bars, gels, real food, electrolyte tablets
steps: Eat a proper carbohydrate breakfast 2-3 hours before.
Start eating within the first 45 minutes, before you want to.
Target 60-90g of carbohydrate an hour on rides over 2 hours.
Set a timer or eat at every junction — do not rely on remembering.
Drink 500-750ml an hour, more in heat, and add electrolytes over 90 minutes.
Mix the food types: something solid early, gels later when the stomach is less willing.
Plan a café or shop stop for anything over 3 hours and top the bottles up.
Practise the exact fuelling plan on training rides before using it in an event.
Eat within 30 minutes of finishing: carbohydrate plus protein.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Indoor Trainer Session
instructions.description: Making turbo sessions productive and bearable.
instructions.warnings: You sweat far more indoors. Protect the frame and headset from sweat — it corrodes bearings quickly.
instructions.equipment: Fan, towel, two bottles, sweat cover, mat
steps: Set up a powerful fan pointed at your chest and face. This is not optional.
Towel over the bars and top tube, or a proper sweat cover.
Mat underneath to catch drips and reduce noise.
Two full bottles within reach before you start.
Warm up longer than outdoors, 15-20 minutes (401).
Choose a structured session — indoor time is best spent on intervals (405, 406).
Stand up for 30 seconds every 10 minutes to relieve saddle pressure.
Keep the room cool; open a window.
Cool down properly rather than stopping dead (403).
Wipe the bike and floor down immediately afterwards.
instructions.notes: One focused hour indoors is worth two distracted hours outdoors for threshold work.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Chain Cleaning and Lubrication
instructions.description: The maintenance job with the biggest effect for the least effort.
instructions.warnings: Never get degreaser into the hub, bottom bracket or headset bearings. Keep it on the chain.
instructions.equipment: Degreaser, chain cleaning tool or brushes, rags, chain lube, chain wear checker
steps: Put the bike in a stand or lean it so the cranks turn freely.
Shift to the smallest sprocket and the big chainring.
Apply degreaser to the chain and work it in, backpedalling several turns.
Scrub with a brush, including between the plates.
Clean the cassette with a rag pulled between the sprockets, and the jockey wheels with a pick.
Rinse sparingly with water, avoiding the bearings.
Dry the chain completely — this matters more than people think.
Apply one drop of lube to each roller, backpedalling slowly through the whole chain.
Leave it 10 minutes to penetrate, then wipe all the excess off the outside.
Check chain wear with a gauge; replace at 0.5% for 11/12-speed, 0.75% for older.
instructions.notes: Excess lube on the outside collects grit and wears the chain faster than no lube at all.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Roadside Puncture Repair
instructions.description: Fixing a flat at the side of the road, quickly.
instructions.warnings: Get right off the road first. Find a safe spot even if it means walking a hundred metres on a flat.
instructions.equipment: Spare tube, tyre levers, pump or CO2, patch kit, multitool
steps: Move somewhere safe and well off the road.
Note the tyre position relative to the valve — it helps find what caused it.
Release the brake if rim brakes, and remove the wheel.
Deflate fully and unseat one bead with levers, working away from the valve.
Remove the tube.
Run a finger carefully round the inside of the tyre to find the glass or thorn. This is the step people skip and then puncture again in a kilometre.
Check the rim tape is in place and undamaged.
Partially inflate the new tube so it holds its shape, and fit it starting at the valve.
Work the tyre bead back on by hand as far as possible; use levers only at the very end and carefully.
Check the bead is seated evenly all the way round on both sides before inflating.
Inflate to pressure, refit the wheel, close the quick-release, reconnect the brake, and spin the wheel to check.
instructions.afterUse: Patch the old tube at home so you always carry a spare.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Tyre Pressure Setup
instructions.description: Setting pressure for the rider, the tyre and the surface.
instructions.warnings: Maximum pressure on the sidewall is a limit, not a recommendation. Most people ride far too hard.
instructions.equipment: Floor pump with an accurate gauge
steps: Check pressures before every ride or two — tubes lose several psi a week, latex much more.
Start from the tyre width: wider tyres need much less pressure.
As a rough guide for a 70-80kg rider: 25mm around 80-90 psi, 28mm around 70-80, 32mm around 55-65, gravel 35-40mm around 30-40.
Run slightly less at the front than the rear, typically 5 psi less.
Reduce pressure for rough surfaces, wet roads and comfort; add a little for smooth roads.
For tubeless, do not go so low that the tyre burps in corners.
Check the tyre for cuts and embedded debris while the pump is in your hand.
Note what works and adjust in small steps rather than large ones.
instructions.notes: Lower pressure is usually faster on real roads as well as more comfortable. The rock-hard tyre is a myth worth abandoning.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Brake Check and Pad Adjustment
instructions.description: Keeping the brakes doing their one job.
instructions.warnings: Never get oil, degreaser or chain lube on a disc rotor or pad. A contaminated pad is a replaced pad.
steps: Squeeze both levers hard: firm bite point, no travel to the bar, no sponginess.
Rim brakes: check pad wear against the wear line; check they hit the rim squarely and not the tyre.
Rim brakes: set a slight toe-in so the front of the pad touches first, to stop squeal.
Disc brakes: check pad thickness — under about 1mm of material means replace.
Disc brakes: check the rotor is straight and clean; clean with isopropyl alcohol only.
Check the rotor bolts are tight.
Check cables for fraying at the lever and the caliper, or hoses for weeping fluid.
Adjust cable tension with the barrel adjuster so the bite point is where you want it.
Test both brakes hard at walking pace before riding properly.
instructions.maintenance: Hydraulic systems need bleeding roughly annually, or whenever the lever feels spongy.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Gear Indexing Adjustment
instructions.where: Workshop with the bike in a stand
instructions.description: Getting the rear derailleur shifting cleanly again.
instructions.warnings: If the hanger is bent, no amount of indexing will fix it. Check that first or you will chase the problem forever.
steps: Put the bike in a stand so you can turn the cranks.
Check the derailleur hanger is straight by sighting from behind.
Shift to the smallest sprocket and release cable tension at the barrel adjuster.
Set the high limit screw so the jockey wheel sits directly under the smallest sprocket.
Pull the cable taut by hand and clamp it.
Shift up one sprocket. If it hesitates, turn the barrel adjuster anticlockwise a quarter turn; if it overshoots, clockwise.
Work up and down the whole cassette, adjusting a quarter turn at a time.
Set the low limit screw so it cannot go past the largest sprocket into the spokes.
Set the B-tension screw so the top jockey wheel clears the largest sprocket by a few millimetres.
Check every gear under light pedalling load, both directions.
instructions.afterUse: A new cable stretches. Re-check indexing after the first ride on a fresh cable.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Bike Fit Self-Check
instructions.description: A periodic check that the bike still fits you.
instructions.warnings: Change one thing at a time and ride it for a week. Changing three things means learning nothing.
instructions.equipment: Trainer, plumb line or phone app, tape measure, allen keys
steps: Note all your current measurements before touching anything, so you can go back.
Saddle height: heel on the pedal at the bottom of the stroke, leg should be just straight without rocking the hips.
Alternatively, aim for around 25-35 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the stroke.
Saddle fore-aft: with cranks horizontal, a plumb line from the front of the forward knee should fall near the pedal axle.
Saddle level: start dead level and adjust only a degree or two if needed.
Reach: a slight bend in the elbows, shoulders relaxed, no locked arms.
Bar height: higher for comfort, lower for aerodynamics — be honest about your flexibility.
Cleat position: ball of the foot roughly over the pedal axle, with the foot in its natural rotation.
Check for symptoms: knee pain at the front means saddle likely too low, at the back too high; numb hands mean too much weight forward.
instructions.afterUse: Note every change with the date, so a problem can be traced back.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Bike Wash and Post-Ride Care
instructions.description: Cleaning the bike without damaging it.
instructions.warnings: Never use a pressure washer. It drives water straight past the bearing seals and into the hubs and bottom bracket.
instructions.equipment: Bucket, bike-specific cleaner, brushes, sponges, degreaser, rags, lube
steps: Rinse gently with low-pressure water to shift loose dirt.
Apply degreaser to the chain, cassette and chainrings only, and let it work (412).
Wash the frame with bike cleaner and a soft sponge, top down.
Use separate brushes for the drivetrain and the frame — never the same one.
Clean the brake surfaces last with a dedicated clean cloth.
Rinse thoroughly from the top down, low pressure, never aimed at bearings.
Dry with a cloth, then bounce the bike gently to shed trapped water.
Lubricate the chain once dry (412).
Wipe the disc rotors with isopropyl alcohol if any cleaner reached them.
Check the tyres for embedded debris while you are there.
instructions.afterUse: After a wet or salty ride, at minimum wipe the chain and re-lube even if you skip the full wash.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Winter Riding Setup
instructions.description: Setting the bike and yourself up for cold, wet months.
instructions.warnings: Road salt destroys drivetrains and frames. Winter riding means washing the bike far more often, not less.
steps: Fit mudguards — for you and for anyone riding behind you.
Fit wider tyres with more puncture protection and drop the pressure a little (414).
Switch to a wet-weather chain lube, which is thicker and stays put.
Check brake pads before winter and carry spares; they wear far faster in the wet.
Fit strong lights front and rear, and carry a spare rear.
Reflective elements on moving parts — ankles and feet are the most visible.
Dress in layers: windproof outer, thermal base, overshoes, long gloves, a cap under the helmet.
Protect the extremities first — hands, feet and head are what end winter rides.
Carry more spares; punctures are much more common in the wet.
Plan shorter loops closer to home rather than one long ride.
instructions.afterUse: Wash the bike after every wet or salty ride, even briefly (418).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Poolside Warm-Up (Dry)
instructions.description: Waking the shoulders up before they take load in the water.
instructions.warnings: Shoulders are the swimmer's weak point. Five minutes on land prevents a lot of trouble.
steps: Arm circles forward, 15, small building to large.
Arm circles backward, 15.
Shoulder shrugs and rolls, 10 each direction.
Band pull-aparts, 15, if a band is available.
Band external rotations, 15 each arm — the rotator cuff work that matters most.
Thoracic rotations, 10 each side.
Cat-cow or standing spinal waves, 10.
Ankle circles and point-flex, 15 each — a stiff ankle ruins the kick.
Streamline stretch against a wall, 3 x 15 seconds.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: In-Water Warm-Up Set
instructions.description: The first part of every swim, done properly.
steps: 400m easy freestyle, building gradually from very easy.
Focus on long strokes and a relaxed catch rather than speed.
200m as 50 kick / 50 drill / 50 pull / 50 swim.
4 x 50m as 25 drill / 25 swim, with 15 seconds rest.
4 x 25m build — start easy, finish fast, with 20 seconds rest.
Check in with your body: shoulders, neck, breathing rhythm.
20-30 seconds rest, then start the main set.
Total roughly 800-1000m before the main work.
instructions.notes: Cutting the warm-up short is the most common reason a main set feels terrible.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Cool-Down Swim
instructions.description: Flushing the arms out at the end of the session.
steps: 200-400m very easy, slower than feels natural.
Mix strokes — backstroke is excellent for opening the chest after freestyle.
Focus on long, relaxed strokes and full exhalation.
Include 50m of easy kicking on your back.
Finish with 50m of sculling to relax the forearms.
Out of the water, gentle shoulder and chest stretches on the poolside.
Rehydrate — you dehydrate in the pool without noticing.
Rinse off and change promptly (519).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Technique Drill Set — Freestyle
instructions.description: Working on the stroke rather than just covering distance.
instructions.warnings: Drills done fast are just bad swimming. Slow, deliberate, and stop when the quality goes.
instructions.equipment: Fins optional, kickboard, snorkel optional
steps: Warm up first (501).
Catch-up drill, 4 x 50m: one hand stays extended until the other touches it. Teaches a long front end.
Fingertip drag, 4 x 50m: drag the fingertips along the surface on recovery. Teaches a high elbow recovery.
Single-arm, 4 x 50m: one arm only, other extended, alternating by length. Isolates the catch.
6-1-6, 4 x 50m: six kicks on the side, one stroke, six on the other side. Teaches rotation.
Sculling, 4 x 25m: forearms vertical, feeling for pressure on the water.
Finish with 4 x 50m normal swimming, holding the feeling from the drills.
Count strokes per length and try to hold the count as you get tired.
instructions.afterUse: Note stroke count per length. Falling stroke count at the same speed is real improvement.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Interval Set — 10 x 100m
instructions.description: The classic aerobic set.
steps: Warm up fully (501).
Work out a send-off that gives you 15-20 seconds rest per 100m.
Swim 10 x 100m freestyle on that send-off.
Hold an even pace — the tenth should be within a couple of seconds of the first.
Resist the temptation to blast the first three.
Focus on stroke count staying constant as fatigue builds.
If you cannot make the send-off, add 5 seconds rather than abandoning the set.
Cool down 200-400m easy (502).
instructions.notes: A set that gets slower in the second half was started too fast. That is the lesson, every time.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Threshold Set — CSS Pace
instructions.description: Working at critical swim speed, the swimming equivalent of threshold.
instructions.preparations: You need your CSS pace from a test first (516).
steps: Warm up thoroughly (501).
Main set option A: 8 x 200m at CSS pace with 20 seconds rest.
Main set option B: 20 x 100m at CSS pace with 15 seconds rest.
Main set option C: 5 x 400m at CSS plus 2 seconds, with 30 seconds rest.
The effort should be sustainable but genuinely working — around 85-90% of maximum.
Hold pace exactly rather than starting fast; the discipline is the training.
Count strokes on the first and last rep and compare.
Cool down 300m easy (502).
instructions.afterUse: Retest CSS every 6-8 weeks and update your paces (516).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Sprint Set — 25s and 50s
instructions.description: Short, maximal efforts for speed and power.
instructions.warnings: Full recovery between efforts, or it becomes an aerobic set done badly and you get neither benefit.
steps: Warm up very thoroughly — sprinting cold is how shoulders get hurt (500, 501).
Add 6 x 25m build to fast with full rest.
8 x 25m maximum effort with 45-60 seconds rest.
Focus on a fast turnover but do not let the stroke fall apart.
Push hard off every wall and hold a tight streamline.
Rest 3 minutes.
4 x 50m maximum effort with 90 seconds rest.
Stop the set as soon as times drop off noticeably.
Long easy cool-down, 400m (502).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Continuous Endurance Swim
instructions.description: One long steady swim for aerobic base and open water preparation.
steps: Warm up 400m easy (501).
Swim 1500-3000m continuously without stopping at the wall.
Hold an easy, sustainable, conversational-equivalent effort.
Use open turns rather than tumble turns to keep the rhythm steady.
Focus on rhythm and breathing pattern rather than pace.
Break the boredom by changing focus every 200m: catch, then kick, then rotation, then breathing.
Practise bilateral breathing throughout (510).
Cool down 200m very easy (502).
instructions.notes: Excellent preparation for open water, where there is no wall to rest on.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Pull Set with Buoy
instructions.description: Isolating the upper body to build strength and feel.
instructions.warnings: Paddles magnify both good and bad technique, and load the shoulders considerably. Introduce them gradually.
instructions.equipment: Pull buoy, paddles, band optional
steps: Warm up fully (501).
Fit the pull buoy between the thighs and keep the legs still.
8 x 100m pull with 20 seconds rest, focusing on a high-elbow catch.
Add paddles for the second half of the set only, if you use them.
Feel for pressure on the forearm, not just the hand.
Keep the stroke long — the buoy makes it easy to shorten and rush.
Add an ankle band for a harder version, which exposes any hip drop immediately.
Finish with 4 x 50m swimming normally, keeping the same catch feeling.
Cool down 200m (502).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Kick Set
instructions.description: The part everyone skips, which is why everyone has a weak kick.
steps: Warm up first (501).
Kick from the hips, not the knees. Small, fast, with a loose ankle.
8 x 50m kick on a board with 20 seconds rest.
4 x 50m kick on your back with arms at your sides — good for feeling the hip drive.
4 x 25m vertical kicking in deep water, 30 seconds each, hands out of the water for the hard version.
4 x 50m kick on your side, one arm extended, alternating sides.
Point the toes; a flexed foot acts as a brake.
Finish with 4 x 50m swim, feeling the legs contribute rather than drag.
instructions.notes: A weak kick is a body position problem as much as a propulsion one. Sinking legs cost far more than the kick would gain.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Breathing Pattern Drill
instructions.description: Making breathing automatic rather than something you brace for.
steps: Warm up first (501).
Exhale continuously underwater. The most common fault is holding the breath and then having to exhale and inhale in one turn.
4 x 50m breathing every 3 strokes — bilateral.
4 x 50m alternating: 25m breathing to the left only, 25m to the right only.
Notice which side feels worse. That is the side to work on.
4 x 50m as 3/5/3/7 pattern by length, to build comfort with less air.
2 x 100m breathing every 3, focusing on turning the head just enough to keep one goggle in the water.
Practise not lifting the head — breathe into the bow wave.
Finish with 200m easy, holding a relaxed bilateral pattern.
instructions.notes: Bilateral breathing keeps the stroke symmetrical and is essential in open water where the swell may come from one side.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Open Water Swim Preparation
instructions.description: The differences between a pool and a lake or sea, prepared for.
instructions.warnings: Never swim alone in open water. Use a supervised venue or swim with someone on the shore or a kayak, and always wear a tow float.
instructions.equipment: Wetsuit, brightly coloured cap, tow float, goggles plus spare, anti-chafe balm
steps: Check the venue rules, the water temperature and the forecast.
Never swim alone. Tell someone your plan and expected time.
Wear a bright cap and a tow float so you are visible.
Enter gradually and let the face acclimatise — cold water shock is real and the first two minutes are the risky ones.
Float for a moment and get the breathing under control before starting to swim.
Start slowly; the heart rate is higher than in a pool for the same effort.
Practise sighting from the start (512).
Swim parallel to the shore rather than out and back, so you are always near an exit.
Know your exit point and check it as you swim.
Get out before you are cold, not when you are.
instructions.afterUse: Warm up gradually afterwards with dry layers and a warm drink. Do not get straight into a hot shower.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Sighting Drill for Open Water
instructions.description: Swimming straight without a black line to follow.
steps: Practise in the pool first with your eyes closed between sights.
Sight by lifting just the eyes clear — like an alligator — not the whole head.
Time it with the stroke: lift as the hand enters, breathe to the side immediately after.
Two quick looks are better than one long one.
4 x 50m in the pool sighting every 6 strokes.
4 x 50m with eyes closed between sights, checking how straight you actually swim.
In open water, pick a large fixed landmark above the buoy — buoys disappear in chop.
Sight more often in chop and less often in calm water.
Practise breathing to both sides so you can sight either way (510).
instructions.notes: Most people veer consistently to one side. Learn which way you drift and correct for it.

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Wetsuit Swim Practice
instructions.where: Open water or pool if permitted
instructions.description: Getting used to swimming in neoprene before it matters.
instructions.warnings: A wetsuit restricts the shoulders and raises the body. Never do a first wetsuit swim on race day.
steps: Put it on with a plastic bag over each foot and hand — it slides on far more easily.
Work it up in stages, pulling from the inside of the fabric, never the outside, and never with fingernails.
Get the crotch high and the shoulders seated properly — trapped shoulder fabric is what causes restriction and fatigue.
Anti-chafe balm on the neck, wrists and ankles. Not petroleum jelly, which degrades neoprene.
Swim easy for 10 minutes to get used to the buoyancy and the different body position.
Expect a shorter, higher stroke — the legs will float more so kick less.
Practise removing it fast: unzip, pull to the waist while walking, then step out.
Rinse it in fresh water immediately after every swim.
instructions.afterUse: Dry inside out, out of direct sun, on a wide hanger. Never fold on a crease (223).

revisionHistory.changes: Created — imported from the starter library

instructions.title: Tumble Turn Practice
instructions.description: Learning or sharpening the flip turn.
steps: Practise the somersault alone in mid-pool first, exhaling through the nose throughout.
Then practise from a push, somersaulting without the wall.
Judge the distance: start the turn about one arm-length plus a bit from the wall.
Take the last stroke, drop the chin to the chest and tuck hard.
